title: Identity vs Logical Equality
summary: Deep dive into the core architectural distinction: Object Identity (memory location) vs Logical Equality (business state equivalence).
learningObjectives: Differentiate Object Identity (heap memory location) from Logical Equality (value equivalence)
Identify when a class should maintain default identity equality vs when it must override logical equality
Trace how Java collection data structures utilize identity vs logical equality
expectedOutcomes: You can articulate when an object is an Entity (identity-based) vs a Value Object (logical-equality-based)
You know how to inspect raw system identity hashes independent of custom hash codes

activities.title: Practical Context: Distinguishing Entities from Value Objects

realWorldMetaphor.scenario: Pull two \$20 bills from your wallet. Bill A and Bill B are two distinct physical pieces of paper with different serial numbers. But if you owe a friend \$20, they do not care whether you hand them Bill A or Bill B. In commerce, all \$20 bills have *logical equality*. Now consider your Passport. Even if another citizen is also named 'John Smith' and born on the exact same date, their passport has a different identity. You cannot travel on their passport. That is *identity*.
realWorldMetaphor.mapping: Value objects (Money, Coordinates, Dates) care about Logical Equality (`.equals()`). Stateful runtime agents (Threads, Sockets, Windows, Database Connections) care about Identity (`==`).
realWorldMetaphor.takeaway: Logical equality compares interchangeable values; identity tracks unique, non-interchangeable entities.

activities.content:
In Domain-Driven Design and enterprise engineering, classes are partitioned into Entities and Value Objects.

An Entity has a continuous lifecycle identity, while a Value Object is defined purely by its attributes.

Knowing when to preserve default reference equality versus overriding `equals()` is essential for proper domain modeling.

activities.title: Identity vs Logical Equality: Definition and Value Object Architecture
Comparing Identity Hash vs Logical Equality
activities.explanation: m1 and m2 are logically equal because their amounts and currencies match, even though they possess distinct identity hash codes and memory addresses.

stepByStepWalkthrough.description: `m1` and `m2` are allocated separately in heap memory.
`m1 == m2` evaluates to `false` because their memory addresses differ.
`m1.equals(m2)` evaluates to `true` because amounts ($20.0) and currencies (USD) match.
`System.identityHashCode()` confirms both objects have distinct JVM identity hashes.

activities.title: IdentityHashMap vs Standard HashMap
activities.explanation: Standard HashMap groups keys by logical equals(), while IdentityHashMap strictly differentiates keys by memory reference identity (==).

stepByStepWalkthrough.description: In `identityMap`, `c1` and `c2` are treated as distinct keys because `c1 == c2` is false.
Demonstrates the practical difference between value equivalence and object identity in collections.

activities.title: Identity vs Logical Equality Mastery Quiz

questions.question: What is the difference between an Entity and a Value Object in domain design?
options: An Entity is defined by ongoing identity; a Value Object is defined purely by its attribute values
Value Objects are always stored in database tables
questions.explanation: Entities have identity (e.g. User with userId); Value Objects are immutable values defined by attributes (e.g. Money, Date).

questions.question: Which of the following classes should deliberately NOT override equals() and retain default identity comparison?
questions.explanation: Thread represents an active runtime process; two threads are never logically identical, so identity equality is appropriate.

questions.question: What does System.identityHashCode(obj) return?
options: The custom hashCode() defined by the class
The exact hashCode that would be returned by default java.lang.Object.hashCode(), regardless of whether hashCode() was overridden
questions.explanation: System.identityHashCode(obj) returns the default Object.hashCode() derived from the JVM identity, bypassing any custom hashCode().

questions.question: How does java.util.IdentityHashMap compare keys?
questions.explanation: IdentityHashMap intentionally breaks the Map contract by using == and System.identityHashCode for key comparison.

questions.question: If two objects have the exact same memory address (a == b), what MUST be true about their logical equality (a.equals(b))?
options: a.equals(b) MUST return true (assuming non-null reflexive contract)
questions.explanation: By the reflexivity rule, an object must always equal itself.

questions.question: If `a.equals(b)` is true, is `a == b` guaranteed to be true?
options: No, two distinct heap objects can hold equal field contents
questions.explanation: Logical equality does not imply identity equality. Two separate objects can contain identical data.

questions.question: Why does a compiler's symbol table often use IdentityHashMap?
options: To treat distinct syntax tree nodes with identical text as separate unique tokens
questions.explanation: Compilers must track unique AST nodes based on pointer identity, even if two nodes have identical variable names.

questions.question: What is an 'Aliasing Bug'?
options: Accidentally having two variables point to the same mutable object, so mutations via one variable unintentionally modify the other
A typo in a variable name
questions.explanation: Aliasing occurs when two references share the same mutable heap object, causing unintended side effects.

questions.question: In Java records (introduced in Java 14), how is equals() implemented by default?
options: Value-based logical equality comparing all record components
questions.explanation: Records automatically generate value-based equals() comparing every record component for logical equality.

questions.question: When is it appropriate for an instantiable class to NOT provide a logical equals method?
options: When instances represent active agents, threads, windows, or connections rather than data values
Whenever you want to save typing
When the class has more than 3 fields
questions.explanation: Active system components (Threads, Streams, Sockets) are distinguished by identity, not value equivalence.

activities.title: Identity vs Logical Equality Interview Focus

questions.question: How do you decide whether a new class needs an overridden equals() method or should retain default identity?
questions.answer: Ask: 'Is this a Value Object or an Active Entity?' If it represents descriptive data or a value (e.g. `Coordinate`, `Money`, `Address`, `ComplexNumber`), override `equals()` to provide logical equality. If it represents an active entity, service, or resource with unique lifecycle (e.g. `Thread`, `FileChannel`, `OrderProcessor`), retain default identity.
questions.expectedAnswer: Ask: 'Is this a Value Object or an Active Entity?' If it represents descriptive data or a value (e.g. `Coordinate`, `Money`, `Address`, `ComplexNumber`), override `equals()` to provide logical equality. If it represents an active entity, service, or resource with unique lifecycle (e.g. `Thread`, `FileChannel`, `OrderProcessor`), retain default identity.
questions.keyTakeaway: Value objects require logical equality; active resources and entities rely on identity.
keyPoints: Value objects require logical equality; active resources and entities rely on identity.

questions.question: Why does IdentityHashMap exist in the JDK if it violates the Map contract?
questions.answer: `IdentityHashMap` is designed for specialized graph-traversal algorithms, serialization frameworks, and compilers where you need to detect object cycles or track distinct object instances regardless of whether their contents match.
questions.expectedAnswer: `IdentityHashMap` is designed for specialized graph-traversal algorithms, serialization frameworks, and compilers where you need to detect object cycles or track distinct object instances regardless of whether their contents match.
questions.keyTakeaway: IdentityHashMap is specialized for graph traversal, cycle detection, and serialization.
keyPoints: IdentityHashMap is specialized for graph traversal, cycle detection, and serialization.

questions.question: How does `System.identityHashCode()` differ from `object.hashCode()`?
questions.answer: `object.hashCode()` invokes whatever overridden method the class defined. `System.identityHashCode(object)` bypasses any overridden method and invokes the original `java.lang.Object.hashCode()` implementation directly.
questions.expectedAnswer: `object.hashCode()` invokes whatever overridden method the class defined. `System.identityHashCode(object)` bypasses any overridden method and invokes the original `java.lang.Object.hashCode()` implementation directly.
questions.keyTakeaway: System.identityHashCode() returns the raw identity hash regardless of overrides.
keyPoints: System.identityHashCode() returns the raw identity hash regardless of overrides.

questions.question: What is the relationship between Immutability and Value Objects?
questions.answer: Value Objects should almost always be immutable. If an object's identity is defined entirely by its values, mutating those values effectively turns it into a different value, which causes massive bugs if used as keys in hash collections.
questions.expectedAnswer: Value Objects should almost always be immutable. If an object's identity is defined entirely by its values, mutating those values effectively turns it into a different value, which causes massive bugs if used as keys in hash collections.
questions.keyTakeaway: Value objects whose equality depends on field values should be made immutable.
keyPoints: Value objects whose equality depends on field values should be made immutable.

questions.question: How do Java 14+ Records embody the concept of Value-Based equality?
questions.answer: Records are transparent carriers for immutable data. The compiler automatically synthesizes a canonical `equals()` and `hashCode()` that compares every component field for logical equivalence.
questions.expectedAnswer: Records are transparent carriers for immutable data. The compiler automatically synthesizes a canonical `equals()` and `hashCode()` that compares every component field for logical equivalence.
questions.keyTakeaway: Records provide automatic value-based equality for transparent data carriers.
keyPoints: Records provide automatic value-based equality for transparent data carriers.

questions.question: Can two objects with different memory addresses produce the exact same System.identityHashCode()?
questions.answer: Yes! Due to the Pigeonhole Principle, mapping 64-bit heap addresses into a 32-bit integer means hash collisions can and do happen even in `System.identityHashCode()`.
questions.expectedAnswer: Yes! Due to the Pigeonhole Principle, mapping 64-bit heap addresses into a 32-bit integer means hash collisions can and do happen even in `System.identityHashCode()`.
questions.keyTakeaway: System.identityHashCode is an int and can collide across distinct memory addresses.
keyPoints: System.identityHashCode is an int and can collide across distinct memory addresses.

activities.title: Identity vs Logical Equality Checklist
items: I clearly distinguish Object Identity (address) from Logical Equality (value).
I keep default identity equality for active entities (Threads, Sockets, Services).
I override equals() for Value Objects (Money, Date, Coordinates).
I know how IdentityHashMap compares keys using == instead of .equals().
I know how to call System.identityHashCode(obj) to inspect raw identity hash.
I make Value Objects immutable to avoid breaking hash collections.
I understand that Java records synthesize value-based equality automatically.
I understand how aliasing occurs when reference variables are assigned.
I know that identity equality (==) implies logical equality (.equals()).
I know that logical equality (.equals()) does NOT imply identity equality (==).

practiceProblems.title: Value Object Color vs Resource Thread Equality
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Demonstrate the difference between a Value Object (logical equality) and an Active Resource (identity equality). Complete `RgbColor.equals` to compare `red`, `green`, and `blue`. Verify that two color objects with identical values are equal, whereas two `Thread` objects are not equal.
practiceProblems.expectedOutput:
Colors logically equal: true
Threads logically equal: false
hints: RgbColor is a Value Object: implement equals comparing red, green, and blue.
Thread inherits default identity Object.equals, so two threads are never equal.

practiceProblems.title: Immutable Currency Exchange Value Object
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
Build an immutable `CurrencyRate` value object from scratch:
1. Class `CurrencyRate`: holds `private final String pair` (e.g. "EUR/USD") and `private final double rate`.
   - Constructor initializes both.
   - Override `equals(Object obj)`: two rates are equal if pair matches and `Double.compare(this.rate, other.rate) == 0`.
   - Method `public String toString()` returns `pair + ' @ ' + rate`.
2. In `Main`, create r1 = CurrencyRate("EUR/USD", 1.0850) and r2 = CurrencyRate("EUR/USD", 1.0850).
3. Print `'Identity equal (==): ' + (r1 == r2)`.
4. Print `'Logical equal (.equals): ' + r1.equals(r2)`.
practiceProblems.expectedOutput:
Identity equal (==): false
Logical equal (.equals): true
hints: r1 == r2 is false because they are distinct heap allocations.
r1.equals(r2) is true because pair and rate are logically identical.

practiceProblems.title: Identity Map vs Value Map Dual Key Registry
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
Demonstrate the behavior of standard `HashMap` vs `IdentityHashMap` from scratch:
1. Class `ConfigNode`: holds `private String nodeName`. Constructor initializes it.
   - Override `equals(Object obj)`: matches if nodeName matches.
   - Override `hashCode()`: returns `nodeName.hashCode()`.
2. In `Main`:
   - Create node1 = new ConfigNode("cluster.primary");
   - Create node2 = new ConfigNode("cluster.primary");
   - Insert both into a standard `java.util.HashMap<ConfigNode, String>` with values "Value 1" and "Value 2". Print `'Standard Map size: ' + map.size()`.
   - Insert both into an `java.util.IdentityHashMap<ConfigNode, String>` with values "Value 1" and "Value 2". Print `'Identity Map size: ' + identityMap.size()`.
practiceProblems.expectedOutput:
Standard Map size: 1
Identity Map size: 2
hints: Standard HashMap collapses n1 and n2 because n1.equals(n2) is true.
IdentityHashMap keeps both because n1 == n2 is false.

practiceProblems.title: Bug Hunt: Accidental Identity Comparison in Data Record
practiceProblems.problemStatement: A developer forgot to override `equals()` on a data record `GeoPoint`. When a customer checks if their saved location is in `visitedList`, `contains()` fails because default `Object.equals` falls back to reference identity `==`! Fix `GeoPoint` by overriding `equals(Object obj)` to compare `latitude` and `longitude`.
hints: Implement equals(Object obj) comparing latitude and longitude.

practiceProblems.title: System Identity Hash Code Discrepancy Analyzer
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
Build a diagnostic class comparing custom object hash codes against raw system identity hashes from scratch:
1. Class `DiagnosticItem`: holds `private int id` and `private String tag`.
   - Constructor initializes both.
   - Override `equals(Object obj)`: matches if id and tag match.
   - Override `hashCode()`: returns `java.util.Objects.hash(id, tag)`.
2. Class `HashDiscrepancyAnalyzer`: method `public static void analyze(DiagnosticItem a, DiagnosticItem b)`:
   - Prints `'Logical equals: ' + a.equals(b)`.
   - Prints `'Custom Hash matching: ' + (a.hashCode() == b.hashCode())`.
   - Prints `'Identity Hash matching: ' + (System.identityHashCode(a) == System.identityHashCode(b))`.
3. In `Main`, create item1 = new DiagnosticItem(500, "ALPHA") and item2 = new DiagnosticItem(500, "ALPHA").
4. Run `HashDiscrepancyAnalyzer.analyze(item1, item2)`.
practiceProblems.expectedOutput:
Logical equals: true
Custom Hash matching: true
Identity Hash matching: false
hints: item1 and item2 have matching logical equals and matching custom hashCode.
System.identityHashCode(a) != System.identityHashCode(b) because they occupy distinct heap addresses.
